A grace note is a small note printed before a main note. An ornament is a sign (a trill, a
mordent, a turn) that stands for a short group of notes. Neither tells you exactly *when* the
extra notes sound or *how long* they last. The answer depends on the period and the style, and
for older music it comes from what performers and teachers of the time wrote down.

The main question is the same in every style: **does the grace note fall on the beat, taking
time from the main note, or just before the beat, taking time from the note before?**

Many composers and teachers answered that question in print, in tables of their signs with the
notes written out underneath. This page gives eight of those tables as their authors wrote them,
read from the original prints and manuscripts, from Bach (1720) to Hummel (1828), alongside how
the signs were used in practice, and the very different habits of Irish traditional music and of
jazz and blues.

**How to use the page.** Each sign is shown twice: as written, and played out the way the
source writes it, moved onto the note C so the tables can be compared. Press **▶** on either to
hear the played-out notes. Small print under a name gives the page in the source, and says where a
note count or rhythm is our reading rather than the source's. Each part ends with recordings to
hear the style. The Classical Themes page plays grace notes on the beat, the Baroque and Classical
default.

## Two kinds of grace note

| Written | Name | Where it falls | How long |
|---|---|---|---|
| small note, no slash | appoggiatura | on the beat | long: often half the main note, or more |
| small note with a slash | acciaccatura | on or just before the beat | as short as possible |

The slash only became a reliable sign in the 19th century. In Bach and Haydn an unslashed small
note can still be short, and the context decides (Neumann, *Ornamentation in Baroque*;
Rosenblum).

## Bach and the Baroque

In 1720 J. S. Bach wrote a table of ornaments, the *Explication*, at the front of the
keyboard book he began for his son Wilhelm Friedemann. Each sign stands above a quarter note
with the notes it stands for written out below (Bach, *Clavier-Büchlein*). Together with
C. P. E. Bach's *Versuch* (1753) and Quantz (1752), it is the main evidence for how Bach's signs
were played.

### Bach's whole table

Here is the *Explication* entry by entry, each on the note C as Bach wrote it: the sign, and the
notes Bach wrote out beneath it, with his own note values, read from the manuscript (Bach,
*Clavier-Büchlein*, leaf 3v). Both ▶ buttons in a row play the same written-out notes.

Bach's values do not always add up to the quarter note above them: the trill and the mordent stop
short, and the last three entries run over. The table shows the shape of each ornament, not a
count. On a longer note or at a slower tempo a trill goes on longer, and its last note is held
(Neumann, *Ornamentation in Baroque*).

His signs differ in small hooks and strokes that the music font here cannot draw:

- **Trillo:** a short wave of two humps. **Mordant:** a short wave with a vertical stroke through it.
  **Trillo und Mordant:** a longer wave ending in that stroke.
- **Cadence:** a curl standing upright, like a question mark, not the lying ∽ used today.
- **Doppelt-Cadence:** a small hook rising from below into the wave (begin below). **Idem:** a large
  hook coming down from above (begin with a turn from above). Entries 7 and 8 add the closing stroke.
- **Accent:** a small hook just before the note; the realisation shows whether it rises or falls.
- **The last Idem:** a stroke dropping into a long wave.

**Hear it.** The Netherlands Bach Society's *All of Bach* videos are free and well made. Two
show Bach writing ornaments out in full, the best evidence of what his signs meant:

- English Suite No. 2, BWV 807, Bertrand Cuiller: the Sarabande at
  [11:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kPDTyKts0J4&t=692s), then Bach's own ornamented version,
  *Les agréments de la même Sarabande*, at [14:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kPDTyKts0J4&t=856s).
- Italian Concerto, BWV 971, Christine Schornsheim: the Andante, whose melody Bach wrote out
  ornament by ornament, at [4:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wjXCJL8P0rs&t=262s).
- English Suite No. 3, BWV 808, Pierre Hantaï: the Sarabande at [10:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2UxTsFXZsnQ&t=623s).
- Goldberg Variations, BWV 988, Jean Rondeau: [the Aria](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=chQ7cbSUU-s),
  almost every beat ornamented.

### The appoggiatura: on the beat, and long

An appoggiatura is played **on the beat** and takes its length from the main note. C. P. E. Bach's
rule: before a note that divides in two it takes half, and before a dotted note it takes two
thirds (C. P. E. Bach, ch. 2, sec. 2). It is the dissonant note, so it is the louder one,
and the main note resolves it softly.

```{=html}
<div class="ax-pair">
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Written
M:2/4
L:1/8
K:C
{d}c2 B2 | {f}e3 d | c4 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-play>
X:2
T:Played: half of a plain note, two thirds of a dotted one
M:2/4
L:1/8
K:C
dc B2 | f2 e d | c4 |]
</script></div>
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:2
T:Played: half of a plain note, two thirds of a dotted one
M:2/4
L:1/8
K:C
dc B2 | f2 e d | c4 |]
</script></div>
</div>
```

Not every scholar agrees that all of Bach's small notes are long and on the beat. Frederick
Neumann argued that many, especially those filling in a falling third, were short and could
come before the beat (Neumann, *Ornamentation in Baroque*). Treat on the beat as the default,
and use a short or pre-beat grace when the long one would spoil the line or the counterpoint.

### The trill: start on the upper note

Bach's table and C. P. E. Bach both start a trill on the **note above**, on the beat, so the
trill begins with a dissonance like an appoggiatura. A trill on a long note may end with a
turn (*Nachschlag*) into the next note.

```{=html}
<div class="ax-pair">
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:3
T:Written
M:2/4
L:1/16
K:C
Tc4 B4 | c8 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-play>
X:4
T:Played: from the upper note, on the beat
M:2/4
L:1/16
K:C
dcdc B4 | c8 |]
</script></div>
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:4
T:Played: from the upper note, on the beat
M:2/4
L:1/16
K:C
dcdc B4 | c8 |]
</script></div>
</div>
```

### The mordent: main note, the one below, main note

Bach's *mordant* is quick: the main note, the note below, then back, all at the start of the
beat.

```{=html}
<div class="ax-pair">
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:5
T:Written
M:2/4
L:1/16
K:C
Me4 d4 | c8 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-play>
X:6
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/32
K:C
ede6 d8 | c16 |]
</script></div>
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:6
T:Played
M:2/4
L:1/32
K:C
ede6 d8 | c16 |]
</script></div>
</div>
```

### Improvising ornaments

Baroque players were expected to add ornaments of their own, above all on the repeat of a slow
movement. Bach shows how far this could go: after the Sarabande of his English Suite No. 3 he wrote
out a second, ornamented version of the whole tune, *Les agréments de la même Sarabande*. Below is
its opening theme (from the Classical Themes collection), followed by two ways to ornament it that a
Baroque player might choose, and one they would not.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:20
T:Bach, Sarabande, English Suite No. 3 (BWV 808): the theme
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
BA A3 c/B/ | cA ^F3 A/G/ | AE E2 PD>C | B,3 A, G,2 |]
</script></div>
```

**Choice 1, French: graces on the strong notes.** An appoggiatura from above leans on beat 2,
where a sarabande puts its weight. A trill from the upper note goes on the leading tone, and a
mordent goes on the last note of the cadence. The tune stays the same, and each ornament falls on
a note that is a dissonance or a point of arrival.

```{=html}
<div class="ax-pair">
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:21
T:Written
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B{B}A A3 c/B/ | cA T^F3 A/G/ | AE E2 D>C | B,3 A, MG,2 |]
</script><script type="text/plain" data-play>
X:22
T:Played
M:3/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B2 B2A2 A4 c B | c2A2 G^FG^F^F2 A G | A2E2 E4 D3C | B,6 A,2 G,=F, G,2 |]
</script></div>
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:22
T:Played
M:3/4
L:1/16
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
B2 B2A2 A4 c B | c2A2 G^FG^F^F2 A G | A2E2 E4 D3C | B,6 A,2 G,=F, G,2 |]
</script></div>
</div>
```

**Choice 2, Italian: fill in the long notes.** The long notes are broken into running notes
(*passaggi*, also called divisions) that circle the written pitch and move on to the next one.
The notes that fall on the beat are still the written melody, so the harmony underneath doesn't
change. Corelli's slow movements, printed with ornaments added in 1710, are the classic model.

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:23
T:Divisions on the long notes
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
BA AG/A/ Bc/B/ | cA ^F/G/A/^F/ G A/G/ | AE E/^F/G/E/ D>C | B,3 A, G,2 |]
</script></div>
```

**Not appropriate: ornaments everywhere, and on the wrong notes.** Here there's a mordent on
every note, and a trill on the final G, where the cadence comes to rest. A trill adds tension, so
it belongs on the note before the resolution, never on the resolution itself. With an ornament on
every note, beat 2 no longer stands out, and the dance goes with it. C. P. E. Bach warned that
ornaments used too freely are like too much seasoning (C. P. E. Bach, ch. 2, sec. 1).

```{=html}
<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:24
T:Too much, in the wrong places
M:3/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=60
K:Gm
MBMA MA3 Mc/MB/ | McMA M^F3 MA/MG/ | MAME ME2 MD>MC | MB,3 MA, TG,2 |]
</script></div>
```

## France: Couperin and d'Anglebert

The French harpsichordists printed the most detailed ornament tables of all, and Bach's own table
borrows from them. Jean-Henri d'Anglebert's *Pièces de clavecin* (1689) opens with 29 *agréments*:
plain, leaned-on and turned trills (*tremblement simple*, *appuyé*, *cadence*), the *double cadence*
(a turn), the *pincé* (mordent), the *cheute* or *port de voix* (appoggiatura from below or above),
*coulés* filling in thirds, arpeggios, and the *détaché*, a short silence before a trill or a mordent.
Like Bach, he writes every ornament on the beat and starts every trill from the note above
(d'Anglebert).

François Couperin's *L'Art de toucher le clavecin* (1716) explains how his signs are played, and
adds two things the tables do not show. A trill's beats "begin more slowly than they end", and every
pincé, double pincé and trill stops on the main note (the *point d'arrêt*) inside the note's value
(Couperin).

<!-- ornament-table: couperin-1716 -->
```{=html}
<table class="ax-table">
```

## Italy and England: Geminiani and Purcell

Francesco Geminiani's *The Art of Playing on the Violin* (London, 1751) lists fourteen "Ornaments of
Expression" and, unusually, says what each one expresses: a long beat for "Fury, Anger,
Resolution", a soft swelling one for "Horror, Fear, Grief". Six of them change the notes; the rest
are holding the note, staccato, swelling and diminishing, piano and forte, and the "close shake",
which he says "cannot possibly be described by Notes" (it is vibrato, and he wants it often)
(Geminiani).

Henry Purcell's harpsichord *Lessons* (1696, published by his widow) begin with "Rules for Graces":
"you allway's shake from the note above and beat from ye note or half note below, according to the
key you play in". A shake is the upper-note trill; a beat is the English name for a mordent from the
note below. The printed examples are hard to read and are said to contain misprints, so the note
counts below follow the rules more than the plate (Purcell).

## Haydn, Mozart and the Classical style

The Classical sources keep the long appoggiatura on the beat but give the short one more room.
Leopold Mozart's violin method (1756) and Türk's *Klavierschule* (1789) both describe long
appoggiaturas that take half or more of the main note, and short ones that are played quickly
**on the beat**, taking only a sliver of the main note (L. Mozart; Türk, ch. 3).

- **Long or short?** A small note written as a longer value (an eighth before a quarter) is
  usually long. A sixteenth or a thirty-second before a note, a grace before a repeated note,
  or one in a quick tempo is usually short (Türk; Neumann, *Mozart*).
- **On the beat.** Even the short ones fall on the beat in Haydn and Mozart, with the bass.
  Playing them before the beat is a later habit (Brown).
- **Trills.** Most begin on the upper note, as in Bach, but Classical sources allow a
  main-note start when the note before is already the upper note, or when the trill starts a
  phrase (Rosenblum; Neumann, *Mozart*).

### Three treatises, as their authors wrote them

Daniel Gottlob Türk's *Klavierschule* (1789), Leopold Mozart's violin method (1756) and Muzio
Clementi's piano *Introduction* (c. 1801) are the closest we have to Bach's table for Haydn's and
Mozart's world. All three put the appoggiatura on the beat and give it half the main note (more
before a dotted note), and all start the trill on the note above. They differ in the details:
Türk times the short appoggiatura by tempo; Leopold Mozart lets an appoggiatura before a dotted
note take everything but the dot, and allows one grace before the beat, the *passing*
appoggiatura between notes a third apart; Clementi, a generation later, allows a short shake that
starts on the main note, and says composers leave the kind of shake to "the taste and judgment of
the performer" (Türk; L. Mozart; Clementi).

### Haydn's own sign

Haydn's keyboard music has a sign of its own, a turn with a vertical stroke through it, the
"Haydn ornament". What it meant is still argued over, and the sources disagree even on where it
stands: in the slow movement of the E♭ Sonata, Hob. XVI:49 (1790), the first edition (Artaria,
1791) engraves a small cross-like sign over two notes in each of bars 9 and 11, where Haydn's
autograph has a sign that a coarse scan cannot tell from a short trill (Haydn, autograph; Haydn,
Artaria). Modern editions and Somfai's study discuss it; until we have read them, this page gives no
realisation (Somfai).

**Hear four readings of the same Adagio.** Hob. XVI:49, II. *Adagio e cantabile*, on official uploads.
Listen to bars 1-12 (about the first minute) and compare the small notes and signs:

- Ronald Brautigam, fortepiano: [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hGq5VGR_6oQ)
- Alfred Brendel, piano: [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZT5eJcW6RHI)
- Paul Lewis, piano: [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f77tyuwa8Qs)
- Marc-André Hamelin, piano: [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3m7qHE3QU7U)

### Mozart writes it out

Mozart's Sonata in F, K. 332, shows how much a Classical player added. In the autograph, the
Adagio's reprise repeats the opening plainly; in the first edition (Artaria, 1784), printed under
Mozart's eye, the same bars return heavily embellished, with runs of 32nds, triplets and trills
(Mozart, Artaria). Hear it on fortepiano: Kristian Bezuidenhout,
[K. 332, II. Adagio](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1sgfcMXbpQg); the reprise comes about halfway through.

## Hummel, Chopin and the 19th century

Through the 19th century, short grace notes moved **before the beat** in much music, and trills
more and more started on the main note (Brown). The turning point in print is Johann Nepomuk
Hummel's piano method (1828). He says the old rule, the trill from the note above, "was made for
the voice", and that on the piano the weight belongs on the main note: his trill begins and ends on
it, and a start from above or below has to be written as a small note (Hummel).

**Chopin** is the exception pianists remember. His pupils report that he wanted grace notes and
the start of trills played **with the bass note**, on the beat (Eigeldinger). The Polish National
Edition's performance notes spell it out piece by piece: in the Moderato in E (WN 56) the first
grace note is struck with the bass; "all trills without grace notes should begin with the
principal"; and where Chopin writes a small note before a trill, the trill starts on that note,
"simultaneously with the G in the left hand". Yet in the early Contredanse (WN 27) the edition says
to "execute all grace notes in an anticipated manner", before the beat (Ekier). Chopin wanted even
a turn sung: "not a quick gruppetto, but eight notes well sung" (Ekier). Raoul Pugno, who studied
the Chopin tradition in Paris, notes that in the Berceuse a small flat over a trill belongs to its
upper note, and asks for two of its trills "a little longer" and the next one strictly in time
(Pugno).

**Singers** kept the older rule longest. Manuel García's *Traité* (1847) says the appoggiatura in
Italian singing is less an ornament than a matter of the words: it "falls always on the downbeat
and on the long syllable", and can come from any interval, a fifth in Mozart's "andiam" in *Don
Giovanni* (García).

**Hear it.** Recordings by players and singers trained in the 19th century, free on the Internet
Archive:

- Vladimir de Pachmann, Chopin, [Nocturne in B, Op. 32 No. 1](https://archive.org/details/78_nocturne-in-b-major_vladimir-de-pachmann-chopin_gbia0545821a)
  and [Mazurka in F♯ minor](https://archive.org/details/loc-jukebox-285277-mazurka-in-f-sharp-minor) (1912, Library of Congress National Jukebox).
- Ignacy Jan Paderewski, Chopin, [Nocturne in F♯, Op. 15 No. 2](https://archive.org/details/78_nocturne-in-e-sharp-major-op-15-no-2_ignace-jan-paderewski-chopin_gbia7042343a)
  (HMV, 1928; the archive's title says "E sharp").
- Adelina Patti, Bellini, ["Casta diva"](https://archive.org/details/78_castadiva_139_09) (1906), with
  [more of her 1905–06 recordings](https://archive.org/details/adelina-patti): bel canto
  appoggiaturas and turns from a singer born in 1843.

## Irish traditional music

In Irish flute, whistle and fiddle music grace notes are not melody notes at all but
articulations: a **cut** is a flick to a higher note, a **tap** (or strike) a flick to a lower
one, and a **roll** combines them around a long note. They are so short that they have no
rhythmic value of their own and fall right at the start of the main note (Larsen).

## Jazz and blues

Jazz players use grace notes freely and they are rarely written. They come **before the beat**
or across it, in swing time, and they are part of how a phrase is shaped rather than decoration
added on top. Where an arranger does write them, the big-band chart has its own set of signs:
Michele Caniato's checklist of "expressive devices" runs from gliss, rip and bend through shake,
doit, growl, smear, fall, spill and plop to the turn (Caniato).

- **The blue third.** On piano, which cannot bend a note, the minor third is crushed into the major
  third: struck together and the lower one let go, or a quick grace from the minor into the major.
  It stands in for the singer's or guitarist's bend between them (Komara; Hines). Grace from below,
  never from above, or it sounds minor. See [Blues Piano](blues-piano.qmd).
- **Terminal vibrato.** Louis Armstrong starts a long note straight and lets vibrato in towards
  its end; Gunther Schuller calls the trumpet shake "a more extreme way of enlivening and swinging
  the tone" (Schuller). B.B. King's guitar version is the "butterfly" vibrato, from the wrist
  (Koch).
- **Ghost notes and bends** are written as a note in brackets (or an x notehead) and as an arrow
  marked ¼, ½ or full.

In the table below, ▶ plays the slides on a clean electric guitar, so a fall falls and a bend bends, where
notation can only show steps. How far and how fast each one goes is our estimate: players differ.

**Hear it.** Official uploads (label channels):

- Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five, ["West End Blues"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BTxhgmk_ofk)
  (1928): the opening cadenza, then bends and the blue third in the first strain and "hushed
  vibrato on the final A♭" (Edexcel).
- Meade "Lux" Lewis, ["Honky Tonk Train Blues"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FTKJtTaysrA) and
  Jimmy Yancey, ["Yancey Stomp"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x_XTl_vXwiI): crushed notes.
- Thelonious Monk Quartet, ["Misterioso"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3oHjXTZO33g): crushed
  minor seconds (Kelley).
- Count Basie Orchestra, ["April in Paris"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O3-jTzSgU38) (1955):
  falls and shakes from the whole band.
- Duke Ellington, ["Black and Tan Fantasy"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fvKQJt8idKg) (1927):
  growl and plunger, smears.
- Charlie Parker, ["Ko-Ko"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0ajJBNodEYs) and
  ["Parker's Mood"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=25EkxQyQCBk): bebop turns and enclosures, blues
  inflection on alto.
- B.B. King, ["The Thrill Is Gone"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpC69qIe02E) (1969): bends and
  butterfly vibrato.
- Billie Holiday, ["Strange Fruit"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=649wWWkW_1o) (1939): late
  placement and sparing vibrato (Gourse).

## At a glance

| Style | Grace note | Trill starts | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| J. S. Bach (1720) | on the beat, long by default | upper note | J. S. Bach; C. P. E. Bach; Neumann |
| d'Anglebert, Couperin (1689, 1716) | on the beat ("with the harmony") | upper note, leaned on, beats speeding up | d'Anglebert; Couperin |
| Purcell (1696) | forefall / backfall on the beat | "from the note above"; beat from below | Purcell |
| Geminiani (1751) | on the beat, more than half the note | upper note | Geminiani |
| Leopold Mozart (1756) | on the beat, half (all but the dot before a dotted note); passing ones before | upper note | L. Mozart |
| Türk (1789) | on the beat; short ones a 32nd at moderate speed | upper note, even | Türk |
| Clementi (c. 1801) | on the beat, "in general" half | upper note; a short shake may start on the note | Clementi |
| Hummel (1828) | half the note, on the beat; short ones almost nothing | main note | Hummel |
| Chopin | with the bass, on the beat | main note unless a small note says otherwise | Eigeldinger; Ekier |
| Later 19th century | short ones before the beat | main note | Brown |
| Irish traditional | a flick at the start of the note | (rolls, not trills) | Larsen |
| Jazz, blues | before or across the beat, swung | (shakes, falls, doits) | Caniato; Komara; Schuller |

Anglebert, Jean-Henry d'. *Pièces de clavecin ... Livre premier*. Paris, 1689. IMSLP. [imslp.org/wiki/Pi%C3%A8ces_de_clavecin_(Anglebert,_Jean-Henri_d%27)](https://imslp.org/wiki/Pi%C3%A8ces_de_clavecin_(Anglebert,_Jean-Henri_d%27)). "Marques des Agrements et leur signification", read from the 1689 print (IMSLP #110970).

Bach, Carl Philipp Emanuel. *Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments*. Translated and edited by William J. Mitchell, W. W. Norton, 1949. First published as *Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen*, 1753. Ch. 2, Embellishments.

Bach, Johann Sebastian. *Clavier-Büchlein vor Wilhelm Friedemann Bach*. Manuscript, begun 22 Jan. 1720. Yale University, Irving S. Gilmore Music Library. [collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/10991080](https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/10991080). The *Explication unterschiedlicher Zeichen* is on leaf 3v (IIIF image 10991088); the table on this page is read from it.

Barnhart, Scotty. *The World of Jazz Trumpet: A Comprehensive History and Practical Philosophy*. Hal Leonard, 2005.

Brown, Clive. *Classical and Romantic Performing Practice 1750–1900*. Oxford UP, 1999.

Caniato, Michele. *The Jazz Ensemble Companion*. R&L Education, 2009. Table B.10, "Expressive devices".

Clementi, Muzio. *Introduction to the Art of Playing on the Piano Forte*. London, Clementi, Banger, Hyde, Collard & Davis, [1801]. Internet Archive. Eigeldinger, Jean-Jacques. *Chopin: Pianist and Teacher as Seen by His Pupils*. Edited by Roy Howat, translated by Naomi Shohet et al., Cambridge UP, 1986.

Ekier, Jan, editor. *Wydanie Narodowe Dzieł Fryderyka Chopina* (National Edition). Polskie Wydawnictwo Muzyczne. Performance commentaries. Commentary to Various Compositions (WN 27, WN 56); introduction, "Ozdobniki".

García, Manuel. *École de García: Traité complet de l'art du chant*. Part 2, Paris, 1847. IMSLP. [imslp.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_de_Garcia_(Garcia_Jr.,_Manuel)](https://imslp.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_de_Garcia_(Garcia_Jr.,_Manuel)). The appoggiatura, p. 40 (BnF copy, IMSLP #599813).

Geminiani, Francesco. *The Art of Playing on the Violin*. Op. 9, London, 1751. IMSLP. Example XVIII, text pp. [6]-[8] and plate p. 26 (IMSLP #05501).

Gourse, Leslie, editor. *The Billie Holiday Companion*. Schirmer Books, 1997.

Hummel, Johann Nepomuk. *Ausführliche theoretisch-practische Anweisung zum Piano-Forte-Spiel*. Vienna, Tobias Haslinger, 1828. Internet Archive. [archive.org/details/ausfhrlichetheor00humm](https://archive.org/details/ausfhrlichetheor00humm). Part III, "Von den Verzierungen", pp. 393-402.

Kelley, Robin D. G. *Thelonious Monk: The Life and Times of an American Original*. Free Press, 2009.

Komara, Edward, editor. *Encyclopedia of the Blues*. Routledge, 2006. Crushed notes and bends.

Mozart, Leopold. *A Treatise on the Fundamental Principles of Violin Playing*. Translated by Editha Knocker, Oxford UP, 1948. First published as *Versuch einer gründlichen Violinschule*, 1756.

Mozart, Leopold. *Versuch einer gründlichen Violinschule*. Augsburg, 1756. Internet Archive (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy). [archive.org/details/10527451bsb](https://archive.org/details/10527451bsb). Chs. 9-11, pp. 193-242.

Mozart, Wolfgang Amadeus. *Trois Sonates pour le Clavecin ou Pianoforte*, Op. 6 [K. 330-332]. Vienna, Artaria, 1784. IMSLP.
